title: ci: decide whether required_status_checks.strict should be on for master
body:
Split out of gqlc-0qu, which deliberately did not bundle it.

'Require branches to be up to date before merging' (required_status_checks.strict) is FALSE on master. Confirmed again 2026-07-27 while adding codegen-fence to the required contexts; strict was left as-is on purpose.

## Why it matters

With strict false, a PR's green CI can be computed against a base that no longer exists by the time it merges. Observed on PR #421: its CI was computed against a base that #422 had already replaced, and both touched internal/schema/gql. The combined tree was checked by hand and was fine — but nothing forced that check.

## Why it was not just turned on

Turning strict on serialises every merge: each PR must be rebased onto the new master and re-run CI after any other PR lands. With an autonomous loop merging several PRs an hour, and two loops running concurrently as of 2026-07-27, that could become the dominant cost.

## What to decide

Either accept the risk and record why in an ADR, or turn strict on and measure the added wall-clock per merge. A middle option: leave strict off but add a merge-time guard that refuses when the PR's base SHA is not an ancestor of current master AND the two touch overlapping paths.

Whichever is chosen, the reasoning belongs in an ADR, because the current state is an unrecorded default rather than a decision.

title: schema/gql: a repeated property name silently keeps the last declaration and discards the first
body:
`{ id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING }` parses, resolves, and produces a node type with ONE property: `{Name:id Type:STRING Nullable:true}`. The first declaration is gone -- its type and its NOT NULL with it -- and nothing anywhere says so.

Measured at 61a6cd1 with a probe against New().Parse:

    CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH TYPE T AS {
        (:Person { id :: INT NOT NULL, id :: STRING })
    }
    err=<nil>
    node Person props=1
      id -> {Name:id Type:STRING Nullable:true}

The mechanism is one line: listener.properties builds `out := make(map[string]schema.Property)` and writes `out[p.Name] = p` for every element of propertyTypeList, so a repeat overwrites in walk order (listener.go:498-516).

This is the class-2 shape -- a schema that says one thing resolving to a model that says another, with no diagnostic -- and it is the one duplicate gqlc does NOT reject. resolve() rejects a duplicate node type (ErrDuplicateNodeType) and a duplicate edge type (ErrDuplicateEdgeType) on exactly the reasoning that a map keyed by identity cannot hold two things with one key. A property map is keyed by name and has the same problem.

Downstream this is not cosmetic: codegen emits a struct field per property, so the generated Go silently carries the last spelling. An author who edits a property type and leaves the old line behind gets no error from the tool whose job is to catch that.

DECIDING IT NEEDS AN ADR, WHICH IS WHY THIS BEAD DOES NOT SHIP A FIX.

The ISO BNF admits the syntax: <property type list> ::= <property type> [{ <comma> <property type> }...] with no uniqueness constraint stated in the grammar. Whether a repeat is an error is Syntax Rules prose, which lives in the paid PDF gqlc-lir declined to buy. So this is the same bind as ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch and ErrImpliedLabelIsKeyLabel: two defensible readings, and choosing one silently is picking a dialect. The options are

  (a) reject with a new sentinel, consistent with ErrDuplicateNodeType and ErrDuplicateEdgeType and with the no-dialect principle -- rejecting rather than silently choosing is the move ADR 0015 and ADR 0016 both make; or
  (b) define last-wins (or first-wins) precedence explicitly and pin it with a corpus semantic case, which is the honest form of the status quo.

Note (b) is not free either: the status quo is last-wins by accident of map assignment, not by decision, and nothing pins it, so it can flip to first-wins under a refactor with no test going red.

REGARDLESS OF WHICH IS CHOSEN, the current behaviour is unrepresented in the tree today: no corpus entry, no semantic case, no invalid fixture. That is the part this bead measures.

Found by mutation sweep of internal/schema/gql while auditing the harness for fail-open defects (see gqlc-q5z, gqlc-fon, gqlc-d9b).

title: vuln: on a non-release Go toolchain the scan is silently blind to every stdlib advisory
body:
`just vuln` reports success over the entire standard-library half of the scan
when the Go toolchain is a custom build rather than a release. No warning, no
diagnostic, rc=0 — the same fail-open shape bd gqlc-s3lt closed for an empty
walk, one layer further out.

## Single-variable A/B (first-party, 2026-08-17)

Same tree (gqlc at 15e7a365), same tags, same `govulncheck@latest`, same
vulnerability database, minutes apart. Only GOTOOLCHAIN differs:

    GOTOOLCHAIN=local      go1.26.5-X:nodwarf5   ->  "No vulnerabilities found."
    GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.5   go1.26.5 (release)    ->  "Your code is affected by 3
                                                      vulnerabilities from the Go
                                                      standard library."

Arm B names them: GO-2026-6218 (net/url), GO-2026-6089 (net/http), GO-2026-6088
(encoding/xml), plus GO-2026-5942 and GO-2026-5026, with a concrete trace —

    internal/grammar/gql/gen/gql_parser.go:2620:21: gen.GQLParserInit calls
    sync.Once.Do, which eventually calls asn1.Unmarshal

Arm A reports none of them and exits 0.

## Why this matters beyond one machine

This is how the failure was met: `just vuln` was rc=0 locally on both master and
the branch under review, and govulncheck was RED in CI on both. The local gate
agreed with nothing. A developer running it before pushing gets a green that
carries no information about the largest attack surface in the binary, and the
first place the truth appears is a required check on a PR.

It also inverts the usual local/CI story. The normal complaint is that CI is
stricter; here the local gate is not stricter or looser, it is BLIND — the
finding is absent rather than downgraded, so no amount of reading the output
reveals it.

## Mechanism

govulncheck attributes standard-library findings by resolving the toolchain's
version to a `go1.N.P` release the vulnerability database has entries for. A
version string like `go1.26.5-X:nodwarf5` does not resolve, so the stdlib is
treated as having no known advisories at all rather than as unknown. Third-party
module findings are unaffected — both arms report the same module-level results
— which is why the output still looks like a real scan.

## Fix

The recipe should refuse a toolchain whose version it cannot place, by the
branch's own rule that an unmeasurable input is the measurement broken and not a
clean bill of health. Concretely, before scanning:

  - read `go env GOVERSION`;
  - require it to match `^go1\.[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$` (the same shape
    `internal/tools/modscope`'s `releaseTag` already recognises);
  - if it does not, refuse and say that stdlib advisories will not be reported
    under this toolchain, naming GOTOOLCHAIN as the lever.

A pin belongs with it: assert that the scan output contains a standard-library
section at all, so the day the attribution silently changes shape the gate
notices.

title: ci: govulncheck is red on master — the tree calls 3 stdlib advisories fixed in go1.26.6
body:
`govulncheck` is a required check and it is currently RED on master itself, so
every open PR is blocked regardless of content.

## Evidence (first-party, 2026-08-17)

Re-ran master's own last vuln workflow run — run 31368862709, head f4fb1a19,
which had passed on 2026-08-10 — against today's vulnerability database. Same
tree, same workflow, same commit:

    2026-08-10  run 31368862709  f4fb1a19  SUCCESS
    2026-08-17  re-run of same   f4fb1a19  FAILURE

    Your code is affected by 3 vulnerabilities from the Go standard library.

Nothing in the tree changed. The advisories are new.

## Cause

Advisories published against the standard library since 2026-08-10, every one of
them `Fixed in: <pkg>@go1.26.6`:

    GO-2026-6218  net/url        quadratic complexity in resolvePath
    GO-2026-6089  net/http       ReadHeaderTimeout not applied on the h2c check
    GO-2026-6088  encoding/xml   missing recursion depth guard in decode
    GO-2026-5942  net            panic parsing an invalid SVCB/HTTPS RR
    GO-2026-5026  net/http       ASCII-only Punycode labels not rejected (idna)

Called, not merely required — e.g.

    internal/grammar/gql/gen/gql_parser.go:2620:21: gen.GQLParserInit calls
    sync.Once.Do, which eventually calls asn1.Unmarshal

so the accepted-and-uncalled register (bd gqlc-k22l) is the wrong instrument:
`just vuln` refuses called advisories by design and should keep doing so.

## Fix

`go.mod` and `test/data/codegen/go.mod` both pin `go 1.26.5`, and both CI
workflows resolve the toolchain with `go-version-file: go.mod`. Bump both to
`go 1.26.6`, which is released.

## Not reproducible locally

`just vuln` is rc=0 on this machine for BOTH master and every branch, reporting
no stdlib advisory at all. The local toolchain identifies as
`go1.26.5-X:nodwarf5`; govulncheck appears not to attribute stdlib findings to a
non-release version string. So the local gate is silently blind to the entire
standard-library half of the scan, which is worth a bead of its own — a green
`just vuln` on a developer machine does not mean a green `govulncheck` in CI.

title: vuln: every selftest CALL in the vuln recipe is deletable with the gate green
body:
The same two-halves defect gqlc-eo46 documents for `refuse_stale`, measured in
the `vuln` recipe. It is not one instance — it is every `selftest_*` invocation
in that recipe, and it predates the branch that added the newest one.

## Reproduction (lead, first-party, at 620cea66 / PR #813)

Each row deletes ONE line from the justfile and runs `just vuln`:

    delete the `selftest_platformtag` call      rc=0   SURVIVED
    delete the `selftest_tagblind` call         rc=0   SURVIVED

The BODY of each selftest is well witnessed — mutate the assertion inside
`selftest_platformtag` (`*",windows,"*` -> `*",zzneverwindows,"*`) and the gate
goes rc=1 immediately; same for `selftest_tagblind`'s derived-tag assertion. So
both halves of gqlc-eo46's pattern are present here too: the guard works, and
nothing proves it runs.

`selftest_tagblind` predates `fix/vuln-gate-walk-and-fence`, so this is a
standing class the branch extends by one instance rather than one it introduces.
That is why it is filed rather than fixed there.

## Why it does not close in-script

Same regress gqlc-eo46 names: any counter or assertion wrapped around the call
site is itself a line someone can delete, and the recursion does not terminate
inside the script. The close is the same out-of-band move eo46 proposes — run
the recipe against a fixture tree in which the selftest's precondition is
violated, and assert rc=1 with the term named.

Doing it once for the whole family is probably cheaper than doing it per
selftest: a single harness that, for each `selftest_*` function, deletes its
call site, runs the recipe, and requires rc!=0.

## Scope note

Not a defect in what the gates measure — every selftest passes on the real tree
today, and the properties they assert are independently checked elsewhere in the
recipe. The defect is that their continued presence is unenforced.

title: resolver: two resolvedCovers writes are unpinned today and become load-bearing the moment the lane is carried
body:
Mutation testing of `feat/resolver-narrow-plural-endpoints` at 40ce99a7 (28-row
matrix, out-of-tree copy, `go build` green before every run) found two writes to
the `resolvedCovers` lane that SURVIVE deletion with the whole suite green:

- `internal/resolver/scope.go`, the collapse arm of `NarrowPluralEndpoints`:
  deleting `s.resolvedCovers[v] = struct{}{}` while keeping
  `delete(s.nodeCands, v)` changes no test.
- `internal/resolver/resolve.go`, `candidateTypes`' Phase B commit: deleting the
  `else { delete(t.resolvedCovers, n.Variable()) }` arm changes no test.

Both survivals are honest — the comments beside each already say "changes no
answer today and no test can pin it" and enumerate why. The collapse write is
unobservable because `CloseEdges` returns immediately after the pass and the
lane is not carried; the else arm is unobservable because an unlabelled pending
binding is never already in the lane and `newScope` does not seed it from the
carry.

## Why this outlives the branch

Both reasons are stated as properties of the CURRENT call order and the CURRENT
carry, and both are exactly what `gqlc-etj6` proposes to change. Carrying the
lane across a `WITH`, or moving the narrowing relative to the carry check, makes
both lines live — and whoever makes that change gets no red test if they get
either one wrong. The collapse omission would silently mark a correctly-narrowed
singleton as uncovered (lost precision); the else-arm omission would leave a
stale `covered` on a binding a later Phase B iteration demoted (a WRONG type
committed, which is the unsound direction).

So the risk is not that the lines are wrong now. It is that the safety net for
the person who makes them matter does not exist, and the comments that carry the
reasoning are not a gate.

## Fix

Do this as part of `gqlc-etj6` rather than before it — there is nothing to pin
until the lane is observable. When the lane is carried, add one row per write:
a query whose answer differs with and without the write, asserted on the
resolved column type, not on a golden.

## Witness

Mutation ids G16-collapseCovers and G25-phaseB-elsearm, both SURVIVE; the
remaining 20 guards in the same matrix were KILLED by named tests.

title: resolver: describeColumnType panics on a nil list element, the in-package twin of edze's prepare.go fault
body:
Found while auditing `internal/resolver`'s `ResolvedType` type switches for
`gqlc-856f`. Recorded here rather than fixed because the nil posture belongs to
`gqlc-edze`, which `gqlc-856f` was explicitly scoped out of deciding.

`describeColumnType` (`internal/resolver/resolve.go:363`) has a default arm
that returns `t.String()`. That refuses gracefully for a pointer or embedded
form — which is why `gqlc-856f`'s audit passed it — but its `ResolvedList` arm
recurses on `v.Element`, and a nil `Element` is a nil interface, which matches
no arm and reaches `t.String()` on nil.

Measured at 52f8662 via `go test -overlay` (no file added to the tree):

    describeColumnType(ResolvedList{Element: nil})
      -> PANIC: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

`resolvedTypeEqual` is safe on the same input — its `a == nil || b == nil`
guard catches the recursion — and returns false:

    resolvedTypeEqual(ResolvedList{Element: nil}, ResolvedList{Element: ResolvedNode{}}) = false

The two compose into the fault path: `compareBranchColumns`
(`resolve.go:~2050`) calls `describeColumnType` only for columns
`resolvedTypeEqual` reported unequal, so a nil-element list on one branch and a
populated list on the other reaches the panic while building the mismatch
message.

## Reachability: latent, not live

No originator was found. All three `ResolvedList{...}` constructions in
non-test code assign a non-nil `Element`:

- `scope.go:1004` — `ResolvedEdge` or `ResolvedEdgeUnion`
- `resolve.go:1294` — the result of `resolveType`
- `resolve.go:1458` — the result of `unify`

`unify` will *propagate* a nil: `unify(ResolvedUnknown{}, nil)` returns
`(nil, true)`, so `ResolvedList{Element: nil}` is constructible at
`resolve.go:1458` from an already-nil element. That is propagation, not
origination. `describeColumnType` is unexported and reached only through the
resolver's own pipeline, so this is not reachable by an out-of-package caller
the way `internal/codegen`'s sites are.

## Relationship to gqlc-edze

`gqlc-edze` already owns `resolver.ResolvedList{Element: nil}` faulting at
`internal/codegen/prepare.go:1050`, plus the eight typed-nil pointer forms.
This is the same question one package earlier. If `edze` chooses normalisation
at the boundary, this site may be covered for free; if it chooses refusal, this
default arm needs a nil check of its own. Fold into `edze` if it is being taken
whole.

## Acceptance

Either `describeColumnType`'s default distinguishes a nil interface from a type
it does not recognise, or `edze` records that the resolver's own pipeline
cannot originate a nil element and this stays latent by argument rather than by
accident. A regression pin either way.

title: docs: five prose restatements of ResolvedType as a sealed sum survive gqlc-856f
body:
`gqlc-856f` corrected the claim at its source (`internal/resolver/validated.go`)
and `gqlc-h4ug` had already corrected it in
`docs/specs/codegen-sentinel-taxonomy.md` (rows at lines 138 and 222 now state
the unbounded-inhabitant reading accurately). The prose restatements below are
what is left. Each describes `ResolvedType` as sealed/closed:

- `docs/specs/resolver-stage-r0.md:245` — "`ResolvedType` is the sealed sum the
  columns and parameters carry." §3.4's opening sentence.
- `docs/specs/resolver-stage-r5.md:963` — "the sealed sum" in the type-equality
  paragraph.
- `docs/adr/0010-codegen-typed-repositories-from-validatedquery.md:16` — "sealed
  `ResolvedType` sum".
- `docs/specs/codegen-prepare-commits.md:385` — describes a fence row using "a
  test-file-local stub `ResolvedType` implementation that satisfies the sealed
  interface via `isResolvedType()`". The construction described only works
  in-package; from outside, embedding is what obtains the marker.

## A different sum, same reasoning — worth a separate decision

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c5.md:739` says of the **synthesised edge-union
interface in generated code** (not `resolver.ResolvedType`):

    Consumers type-switch on the interface at the call site; the sealed
    sum guarantees exhaustive coverage under `gochecksumtype`.

Two things to check rather than assume: (1) the same
embedding/pointer argument applies to any Go interface sealed by an
unexported marker, including the generated one, so "guarantees exhaustive
coverage" is the same overclaim one layer down; (2) `gochecksumtype` is not in
`.golangci.yml`'s enabled linters, so whatever it would guarantee is not
currently run. Neither is verified here — this bead records them as questions.

## Why filed rather than fixed

`docs/specs/codegen-stage-c5.md` is held by open PR #804
(`docs/c1-bare-arg-spec-drift`). The other four files are unheld, but they are
prose restatements rather than type switches, so they fall outside
`gqlc-856f`'s acceptance criterion, and splitting them across territories
mid-flight buys nothing.

## Acceptance

Each of the four `ResolvedType` restatements either drops "sealed" or says what
the marker does and does not cover, pointing at
`internal/resolver/validated.go`'s corrected comment rather than repeating the
argument. The c5 question is answered either way and recorded.

title: codegen/age: unservedColumn's fall-through comment restates the sealed-sum claim gqlc-856f corrected
body:
`internal/codegen/age/errors.go:423-425`, at the end of `unservedColumn`,
justifies its fall-through with:

    // ResolvedType is a sealed interface, so the switch above is its
    // whole membership; a variant added to the resolver lands here and is
    // dropped rather than emitted through an arm chosen for some other
    // shape.

Both halves are wrong in the way `gqlc-856f` corrected at the source
(`internal/resolver/validated.go`). `ResolvedType`'s unexported marker is not
a seal: a pointer form of any variant satisfies it (value receivers, and a
pointer's method set contains its value methods), and a struct embedding a
variant satisfies it from any package (Go promotes an embedded type's
unexported methods). So the switch above is NOT its whole membership, and the
type reaching the fall-through today is not "a variant added to the resolver"
but a pointer or embedded form of one of the existing eight.

**The behaviour is correct** — the fall-through returns
`"projects " + t.String()`, a non-empty reason, so an unrecognised type is
refused rather than served. Only the comment is wrong. It is the last live
restatement of the claim in Go source after `gqlc-856f`.

## Second, smaller finding in the same file

`internal/codegen/age/errors.go:251`, in `unservedReason`:

    _, union := col.Type.(resolver.ResolvedEdgeUnion)

For `*resolver.ResolvedEdgeUnion` or a struct embedding it, `unservedColumn`
returns a non-empty reason (via the fall-through above) but this assertion
yields `false`, so the `edgeUnion` flag is false for what is in substance an
edge-union column. That flag drives the ranking `unservedReason` documents at
lines 240-248 ("an edge-union column outranks an unserved parameter"). No
panic; the reason text is still produced, only the ranking degrades.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed

`internal/codegen/age/errors.go` is held by open PR #848
(`fix/age-offset-sidecar-hardening`). `gqlc-856f`'s acceptance criterion asks
for a verdict or a filed follow-up per audited site, not a cross-territory
edit.

## Acceptance

The comment says what the seal does and does not cover, and names the
construction that actually reaches the fall-through. Decide whether the
`edgeUnion` ranking flag at :251 should recognise the non-value forms or
whether the degradation is acceptable, and record which.

title: codegen/neo4j: the decoder scope sweep is blind to a whole entity arm going missing
body:
Measured on PR #858 at 428dfb84, reproduced at fa5dade.

`internal/codegen/neo4j/decoder_test.go`'s `DecoderSuite` derives its scope
reference from an emission and compares that emission against its own
re-emission. Two emitter mutations leave the whole package green:

- drop the decode helper for every edge entity (emit none): `./internal/codegen/neo4j/` rc=0
- emit edge structs with no fields at all:                   `./internal/codegen/neo4j/` rc=0

Why each escapes:

- `structFieldTypesOf` dedupes Go types across all emitted structs, so the node
  arms still carry every Go type the probe's widths claim and the edge loss is
  invisible to `TestProbeDeclaresEveryWidthInEveryArm`'s type comparison.
- `decoderScopeOf` compares an emission to its own reference emission, so
  dropping an arm removes the locals from both sides at once and the equality
  still holds. That is the sharp edge `decoder_test.go:212-215` already warns
  about for the width census; it applies to the entity arms too.

Not a silent hole repo-wide: with the edge decode helper dropped, the full
suite is rc=1 — `--- FAIL: TestSentinelTaxonomy` (internal/codegen) and
`--- FAIL: TestConformanceSuite` (internal/codegen/conformance). So the
four-arm guarantee is enforced, just not by the suite whose doc comments
describe it, and `decoder_test.go:316-317` points at the corpus that does.

Scope if anyone takes it: enforce the four-arm guarantee on the emission
rather than only on the parsed schema — e.g. assert per entity kind that a
`decode<Name>` helper exists and that its struct carries a field per declared
property, instead of asserting over a set deduped across all entities. The
trap to avoid is another guard that compares an emission against a reference
derived from the same emission.

Filed as review residue from PR #858 round 2/3; not blocking that PR.

title: ciguard: pin that every .githooks/tests suite is wired into test-hooks and reached from CI
body:
Raised as a nit by the independent review of PR #867
(/tmp/factory/verdict-867.md, ATTACK 4 row M22) with no bead filed at the
time. Implemented alongside bd gqlc-1ekq, which adds 18 rows to
check-pr-closes-test.sh and therefore has a direct stake in that suite still
being run.

MEASURED on master: deleting any one of the five `bash .githooks/tests/*.sh`
lines from the `test-hooks` recipe leaves `just test-hooks` at rc=0. No member
of test-hooks is membership-guarded; lint-hooks-test.sh guards that the
`lint-hooks` RECIPE is reachable from CI, which is a different property.

Fixed by internal/tools/ciguard/testhooks_test.go: three assertions over the
justfile and ci.yml — every *-test.sh in .githooks/tests appears in the
test-hooks recipe body, `test` depends on `test-hooks`, and ci.yml's `test`
job (a required status check) runs `just test`. It lives in the go tests
rather than inside a shell suite because an unwired suite does not run and so
cannot be the thing that notices.

title: resolver: the corpus sweep resolves every cell under regR7, so the registry axis of CALL diagnostics is uncovered
body:
TestCorpusSweepManifest (gqlc-yb0w, PR for #841) crosses 310 fixture queries against 38 fixture schemas, and every one of the 11780 cells is resolved as New(sch, WithRegistry(regR7)). WithRegistry is the resolver's only Option (internal/resolver/resolver.go:48), so the schema axis and the query axis are swept and the registry axis is a constant.

ErrCallArgAssignability and the R7 YIELD column typing arms read the registry. A change to one of those diagnostics that only manifests under a registry other than regR7 — a different signature set, a missing procedure, a different param token — moves no cell in the sweep.

FIX candidates: add a second registry to the cross product (regR7 plus an empty or narrowed registry) and key manifest cells on (query, schema, registry); or bound the claim explicitly and leave the registry axis to the targeted R7 fixtures.

Cost note: the sweep runs 11780 cells in ~0.15s, so a second registry roughly doubles a cheap test and doubles the manifest, which is already 1.4MB.

PROVENANCE: self-review of the gqlc-yb0w branch.

title: resolver: the corpus sweep's accept column digests the marshalled model, so a field no MarshalJSON emits is outside it
body:
TestCorpusSweepManifest (gqlc-yb0w, PR for #841) records an accepting cell as a digest of json.Marshal(ValidatedQuery). Every ResolvedType in internal/resolver/validated.go writes its own MarshalJSON emitting an explicit anonymous struct, so the digest reaches exactly the fields those methods list. A field added to a ResolvedType struct but not to its MarshalJSON is invisible to the sweep's accept column.

This is the SAME bound the existing test/data/resolver/valid/*.validated.golden.json files already carry — TestValid marshals through the same methods — so the sweep is not weaker than what shipped, but it is not stronger on this axis either, and the bead it came from (gqlc-yb0w) is about a quadrant compared on too little.

Same family as gqlc-yb0w itself: a guard structural on one axis (which cells) and bounded on another (what a cell's value records).

FIX candidates: a reflect-based census asserting every exported field of every ResolvedType appears in that type's MarshalJSON output for at least one corpus cell; or fold the check into the existing sealed-sum work (PR #881 holds validated.go and sealedsum_test.go, so this must sequence after it).

PROVENANCE: self-review of the gqlc-yb0w branch, filed rather than fixed because validated.go is held by PR #881.

title: check-pr-closes: a PR that names no bead anywhere is never checked
body:
Found while implementing gqlc-1ekq (PR for bd gqlc-1ekq).

gqlc-1ekq's premise is that dodging the bead id in the branch name is "not a
control: it is invisible, unenforced". Its fix gives the declared alternative
(`Refs: <bead> #<issue>`), so an author who WANTS to say "touches, does not
resolve" now has a checkable way to. It does not remove the undeclared path:
a PR whose body has no Bead:/Refs: line and whose branch carries no id exits
at "No bead on this PR -> pass" having read nothing.

That path cannot be closed from the body alone; closing it means requiring
every PR to declare a bead (or an explicit "no bead"), which is a policy
change with a cost on trivial PRs, and would want the same treatment gqlc-1ekq
got: its own review.

ACCEPTANCE. Decide whether an undeclared PR is a refusal. If it is, the
refusal has to name both escapes (a `Bead:` line and a `Refs:` line) and there
has to be a declared spelling for "this PR is about no bead", with a row each.

title: check-pr-closes: a Bead: line naming a mirror-less bead still overrides a branch that names a mirrored one
body:
Found while implementing gqlc-1ekq (PR for bd gqlc-1ekq).

A body declaration outranks the branch name unconditionally, and that
precedence is deliberate and pinned ("a Bead line in the body overrides the
branch name"). The consequence is that on branch `fix/gqlc-<mirrored>-thing`,
a body line `Bead: gqlc-<some-bead-with-no-external_ref>` resolves to the
mirror-less bead, takes the "no GH mirror -> pass" exit, and the mirrored bead
the branch names is never examined. One line, no diff, nothing in the log.

The new `Refs:` opt-out from gqlc-1ekq does NOT have this hole: it refuses
when the branch names a different bead ("an opt-out naming a bead the branch
does not is refused"). `Bead:` was left alone because tightening it the same
way would newly refuse PRs that legitimately retarget, and because the escape
predates that branch.

ACCEPTANCE. Decide whether a `Bead:` line that disagrees with a bead id in the
branch name is a refusal, a warning annotation, or stays a silent pass; if it
becomes anything louder, a row per verdict in
.githooks/tests/check-pr-closes-test.sh.

title: check-pr-closes: a bolded **Bead:** label is not read as a declaration
body:
Found while implementing gqlc-1ekq / gqlc-zzz5 (PR for bd gqlc-1ekq).

BEAD_IN_BODY is `(?i)Bead:\s*(\S*gqlc-\S*)`. The markdown-bolded spelling used
by this repo's own ADRs — `**Bead:** gqlc-h9n.22`, see docs/adr/0022 line 5 —
puts `**` between the colon and the id, so `\s*` does not reach the token and
the line matches nothing at all. The PR then falls back to the branch name, or
to no bead.

PRE-EXISTING and unchanged by that PR: master's regex `(?i)Bead:\s*(gqlc-\S+)`
misses the same spelling. gqlc-zzz5 closed the backticked and trailing-dot
spellings by widening the captured VALUE; this one is about decoration around
the KEYWORD, which is a different position in the pattern.

Direction matters: unlike gqlc-zzz5's spellings, recognising this one newly
DEMANDS a Closes on PRs that today are unchecked, so it is a widening of the
gate and wants its own review rather than a fold-in.

ACCEPTANCE. `**Bead:** gqlc-x` and `**Refs:** gqlc-x #N` resolve as
declarations. A row per spelling in .githooks/tests/check-pr-closes-test.sh.

title: check-pr-closes: a PR that names no bead anywhere is never checked
body:
Found while implementing gqlc-1ekq (PR for bd gqlc-1ekq).

gqlc-1ekq's premise is that dodging the bead id in the branch name is "not a
control: it is invisible, unenforced". Its fix gives the declared alternative
(`Refs: <bead> #<issue>`), so an author who WANTS to say "touches, does not
resolve" now has a checkable way to. It does not remove the undeclared path:
a PR whose body has no Bead:/Refs: line and whose branch carries no id exits
at "No bead on this PR -> pass" having read nothing.

That path cannot be closed from the body alone; closing it means requiring
every PR to declare a bead (or an explicit "no bead"), which is a policy
change with a cost on trivial PRs, and would want the same treatment gqlc-1ekq
got: its own review.

ACCEPTANCE. Decide whether an undeclared PR is a refusal. If it is, the
refusal has to name both escapes (a `Bead:` line and a `Refs:` line) and there
has to be a declared spelling for "this PR is about no bead", with a row each.

title: check-pr-closes: a Bead: line naming a mirror-less bead still overrides a branch that names a mirrored one
body:
Found while implementing gqlc-1ekq (PR for bd gqlc-1ekq).

A body declaration outranks the branch name unconditionally, and that
precedence is deliberate and pinned ("a Bead line in the body overrides the
branch name"). The consequence is that on branch `fix/gqlc-<mirrored>-thing`,
a body line `Bead: gqlc-<some-bead-with-no-external_ref>` resolves to the
mirror-less bead, takes the "no GH mirror -> pass" exit, and the mirrored bead
the branch names is never examined. One line, no diff, nothing in the log.

The new `Refs:` opt-out from gqlc-1ekq does NOT have this hole: it refuses
when the branch names a different bead ("an opt-out naming a bead the branch
does not is refused"). `Bead:` was left alone because tightening it the same
way would newly refuse PRs that legitimately retarget, and because the escape
predates that branch.

ACCEPTANCE. Decide whether a `Bead:` line that disagrees with a bead id in the
branch name is a refusal, a warning annotation, or stays a silent pass; if it
becomes anything louder, a row per verdict in
.githooks/tests/check-pr-closes-test.sh.

---

## AMENDMENT (PR #901 round 7): the wider variant, which the description above does not cover

The description is written around the *mirror-less bead* variant. There is an
easier and stronger one, reproduced first-party on `master` as well as on the
PR branch, so it is pre-existing rather than PR #901's regression:

    Bead: gqlc-<any well-formed id the export does not carry>

That takes `check-pr-closes.py`'s not-in-export exit (`bead not in export -
skipping`, rc=0). It disables the gate on **any** branch, in one line, and
needs no knowledge of a real bead id — where the mirror-less variant needs one
that exists and has an empty `external_ref`.

That door is held open deliberately: this repo's `.beads/issues.jsonl` trails
the ledger by whole sessions, so a bead created today is legitimately absent,
and PR #901 pins the behaviour with a row (*a bead the export does not carry
does not block the PR*). The rationale is sound. What was missing is that the
consequence was not written down anywhere durable.

**And it can be written invisibly.** `BEAD_IN_BODY` is read over the raw body,
not over `prose_only()`'s, so unlike the `Refs:` marker it is still matched
inside fenced code blocks, HTML comments and `<pre>`/`<code>` blocks. So:

    <!--
    Bead: gqlc-notinexport
    -->

is a gate bypass that no human reading the rendered PR body can see. The only
trace is the one log line in the check run. That asymmetry is deliberate and
argued in the `BEAD_IN_BODY` comment — for a *mirrored* bead a `Bead:` line
ends in a demand for `Closes #N`, so widening where it is read is fail-closed —
but the not-in-export skip is the one exit where the widening is a pass, which
is exactly this issue.

**ACCEPTANCE, extended.** Whatever this issue decides, it has to decide it for
the wider variant and for three carriers, not for the mirror-less variant in
prose alone.

title: bdguard: the git boundary (run, showAtRef, gitRefContaining) has no automated test
body:
internal/tools/bdguard/main_test.go states at the top that it targets check() directly, with no git shellout, and that the git boundary of run() is exercised only by an end-to-end incident replay recorded in a PR body. The stated reason is that earlier attempts to stage a real repo per test occasionally landed git calls in the outer worktree despite GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES.

gqlc-npyp added a third shellout, gitRefContaining, behind the same boundary. It is injected into check() as a func value, so its CALLERS are covered by fakes, but the function itself — cat-file -e, for-each-ref --contains, merge-base --is-ancestor, and the decision to collapse every failure into "" — is verified only by hand. Same standing as showAtRef, which has been in that position since the tool landed.

What a test would have to do: build a scratch repo outside the worktree (t.TempDir plus GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE set explicitly rather than relying on cwd, which is what previously leaked), commit twice, delete the branch, and assert that a referenced sha names a ref and an orphaned one returns "". Also worth pinning: a sha the repo does not have at all returns "" rather than erroring out of the run.

Not blocking: the veto direction means a wrong "" grants no exemption on its own — the other two conditions still have to hold — and a wrong non-empty answer only refuses a declaration, which is loud.

title: bdguard: the reachability veto is inert in CI because the checkout is depth-1
body:
gqlc-npyp's reopened-arm exemption has three conditions. The third — no ref in this checkout contains the declared closing sha — is a veto: it can refuse a declaration, never grant one. It is inert in CI.

.github/workflows/ci.yml uses `actions/checkout@v4` with the default fetch-depth of 1, then `git fetch --depth=1 origin \$BASE_SHA` before `just bd-export-monotonic`. In that clone `git cat-file -e <sha>^{commit}` fails for anything outside the fetched pack, so gitRefContaining returns "" and the veto says nothing. The two conditions that do the work in CI are the base close_reason citation and the updated_at ordering, both of which are answerable from the two files alone; the veto only bites under `just bd-export-monotonic-local`, where the dev worktree has full history and remote-tracking refs.

Making it bite in CI needs a workflow change (fetch-depth: 0, or a targeted fetch of the declared shas), which is outside gqlc-npyp's territory — ci.yml was owned elsewhere in that wave. Weigh it against the reason the job fetches depth-1 in the first place: the comment there says cost is deliberately O(1) in history size. A targeted `git fetch origin <declared-sha>` per entry in .beads/allowed-reopens.txt is O(entries) and keeps that property; a blanket fetch-depth: 0 does not.

Note the veto is weak even with full history: gqlc squash-merges and deletes the branch, so an EARNED close's cited branch sha is orphaned as surely as an unearned one's. It bites on the narrower case where the branch is still pushed and its remote-tracking ref exists.
